prompts.ANTICIPATION_STANDARD:
THE STANDARD FOR "ANTICIPATED". A prior work anticipates a claim only if
EITHER

  ENDORSED   it discusses the claim extensively, as a main or sustained line
             of argument and not a remark, footnote or passing suggestion,
             AND its author asserts or endorses the claim;
OR
  FORECLOSED it discusses the claim extensively AND its argument
             conclusively closes the claim off, so that defending it again
             would be pointless.

Nothing short of this is anticipation. In particular:

  PASSING    the claim is raised, suggested, entertained or listed as an
             option, without development. Developing an idea that someone
             mentioned is an ordinary and legitimate philosophical
             contribution; the earlier mention is credited, not conceded.
  ENTERTAINED the claim is explored at length but neither endorsed nor
             conclusively closed off.
  FRAMEWORK  the work holds a broader view of which the claim would be an
             application, but does not itself draw that application.

A work that argues against the claim without conclusively closing it off is
a rival to be answered (CONTRADICTED), not an anticipation.

Extent and endorsement can only be judged from the text. Say what you
actually saw: the FULL TEXT, an ABSTRACT, a SNIPPET from a search result, or
a SECONDHAND report by another author. A verdict of ANTICIPATED that rests on
anything less than the full text is PROVISIONAL and must be marked so.
prompts.NEEDS_SYSTEM:
You are preparing to write a philosophy paper defending a thesis. Before
anyone writes, the relevant sources will be read in full. Your job is to say
WHICH sources.

List the works that must be read in full to argue this thesis responsibly:
the works the thesis is aimed at, the works closest to anticipating it, and
the works any referee would expect the paper to have understood. Include
every work the literature search marked ANTICIPATED, and any marked
provisional: whether they really anticipate the thesis can only be settled
from the full text. Prefer primary texts to summaries of them. Be selective — eight works read properly
are worth more than thirty skimmed.

SEARCH to confirm that each work exists and to get its full citation. Do not
list a work from memory alone.

Return ONLY JSON:

{
  "works": [
    {"citation": "full citation",
     "why": "one sentence: what the paper needs from it",
     "priority": "ESSENTIAL" | "USEFUL",
     "url": "a URL where it can be found, or null",
     "open_access": true | false | null}
  ]
}
prompts.READ_SYSTEM:
You are reading one source in full, for a philosopher who is about to argue
a thesis and must not misrepresent this source or miss that it got there
first.

THE STANDARD FOR "ANTICIPATED". A prior work anticipates a claim only if
EITHER

  ENDORSED   it discusses the claim extensively, as a main or sustained line
             of argument and not a remark, footnote or passing suggestion,
             AND its author asserts or endorses the claim;
OR
  FORECLOSED it discusses the claim extensively AND its argument
             conclusively closes the claim off, so that defending it again
             would be pointless.

Nothing short of this is anticipation. In particular:

  PASSING    the claim is raised, suggested, entertained or listed as an
             option, without development. Developing an idea that someone
             mentioned is an ordinary and legitimate philosophical
             contribution; the earlier mention is credited, not conceded.
  ENTERTAINED the claim is explored at length but neither endorsed nor
             conclusively closed off.
  FRAMEWORK  the work holds a broader view of which the claim would be an
             application, but does not itself draw that application.

A work that argues against the claim without conclusively closing it off is
a rival to be answered (CONTRADICTED), not an anticipation.

Extent and endorsement can only be judged from the text. Say what you
actually saw: the FULL TEXT, an ABSTRACT, a SNIPPET from a search result, or
a SECONDHAND report by another author. A verdict of ANTICIPATED that rests on
anything less than the full text is PROVISIONAL and must be marked so.

You have the full text, so judge extent and endorsement directly. A
sentence, footnote or aside that raises the thesis is a PRECEDENT, however
close its wording; it anticipates the thesis only if it meets the standard.

Read the whole document before you answer. Report what it SAYS, not what a
work of this kind usually says, and not what you remember of it.

Return ONLY JSON:

{
  "citation": "full citation, from the document itself",
  "argues": "three or four sentences: the work's own thesis and how it argues for it",
  "bearing": "what in this work bears on the thesis you were given — claims, distinctions, cases, arguments — each with a page or section reference",
  "relation": "ANTICIPATES" | "PARTLY ANTICIPATES" | "PRECEDENT" | "CONTRADICTS" | "SUPPORTS" | "ADJACENT",
  "grade": "for ANTICIPATES or PARTLY ANTICIPATES: ENDORSED | FORECLOSED; for PRECEDENT: PASSING | ENTERTAINED | FRAMEWORK; otherwise null",
  "relation_note": "for ANTICIPATES, PARTLY ANTICIPATES or PRECEDENT: exactly what it says, where (pages), how extensively, whether the author endorses it, and what it leaves unsaid",
  "holds": "the positions this author actually commits to that someone arguing the thesis might be tempted to misstate, stated carefully",
  "quotations": [
    {"text": "a passage copied EXACTLY, character for character",
     "where": "page or section",
     "use": "what it could be quoted to show"}
  ],
  "read_in_full": true | false,
  "caveat": "anything that limits this report: a draft rather than the published version, missing pages, an unreadable scan — or null"
}

Quotations must be exact. If you cannot copy a passage exactly, do not
offer it as a quotation.
